source.name: Recovered headline sample
source.scopeNote: Fixed window 2018-05-28 through 2018-12-16 inclusive. The retained sample contains 15 dated Sterling headline records across four playable desks (The Guardian, The Independent, The Sun and BBC Sport). It includes two direct Guardian pages dated 29 May, one Sun print headline reproduced by the Guardian, one Sun web page dated 28 May, and one BBC Sport page. The Foden MailOnline page is comparator context only and excluded because it is about Foden; the January Adarabioyo comparator remains unretrieved and outside this window. Missing records are unknown, not zero; this is not a census and does not establish motive, harm or causation.
source.sampleNote: 15 records retained for Sterling. The Sun print item is a contemporaneous secondary reproduction, while its 28 May web story is a direct original publisher page. Four desks are playable; Foden's verified MailOnline story is source-linked comparison context, not a Sterling row.

evidence.label: publisher report
evidence.text: Sterling explained that the rifle tattoo had a personal meaning connected to his father being killed by a gun; he said he understood why an uncontextualized image could prompt criticism. The tattoo is not evidence of promoting gun use.

evidence.label: publisher report / response
evidence.text: Sterling compared two MailOnline headlines about young Manchester City players buying homes for their mothers, alleging that wording cast Black player Tosin Adarabioyo in a more negative light than white player Phil Foden. The publisher and commentators disputed claims of intent; do not convert comparison into proof of motive or causal link to alleged stadium abuse.

evidence.label: reported allegation
evidence.text: Police and Chelsea said they were investigating an alleged racist incident at Stamford Bridge; no arrest was reported in this account. Allegation and investigation are not an adjudicated finding.

evidence.label: Public-interest chronology: 2018-05-29
evidence.text: The Sun foregrounded an image of Sterling’s rifle tattoo; Sterling publicly explained it as connected to his father’s killing and said it was unfinished. The explanation changes the context needed to assess criticism; it does not settle every reader’s view of the imagery.

evidence.label: Public-interest chronology: 2018-06-01
evidence.text: England manager Gareth Southgate publicly supported Sterling and described the tattoo’s meaning as individual. A relevant institutional response adds context, not a finding about press motive.

evidence.label: Southgate response reported 1 June 2018
evidence.text: The audited publisher headline reports Gareth Southgate’s support for Sterling over the tattoo controversy.

evidence.label: Publisher response reported 11 December 2018
evidence.text: Audited publisher headline reports the response to criticism of coverage.

evidence.label: The Sun print headline (reproduced contemporaneously)
evidence.text: Contemporaneous Guardian report published 29 May 2018 states The Sun placed the tattoo image on that day's front page and gives the reproduced headline. The Independent's contemporaneous page independently says the story was on Tuesday's front page, but the Sun page itself was not recovered. Record this as a print edition, not a Sun web article. Headline and date evidence: Guardian page: first published 29 May 2018; it attributes the front-page wording to The Sun.

evidence.label: The Guardian news
evidence.text: Publisher page shows the exact headline and first-publication timestamp (29 May 2018, 11:10 CEST). It reports the FA response, Sterling's explanation, and The Sun front page. evidence.label: The Sun news-web

evidence.label: MailOnline comparator page, outside subject attribution
evidence.text: The publisher page directly verifies the exact Foden headline and first publication on 4 October 2018 (updated 5 October). evidence.label: Media source · BBC Sport · 2018-12-09
evidence.text: BBC Sport published a page reporting Sterling's criticism of newspaper portrayals of young Black footballers and embedded a clip in which Ian Wright comments on criticism of Sterling. Date basis: hosting_page_publication. This verifies BBC's online publication and embedded clip caption, not a separate broadcast airing or the original upload date of the video. BBC reports Sterling's social post; the article is not itself Sterling's original post.

evidence.label: A reported leader response · Leader column, attributed by contemporaneous reporting
evidence.text: Denied racial bias. This link is the report, not the original leader. Its exact original title and publication metadata remain unverified. It evidences an attributed institutional defence, not proof of motive, truth or owner direction.

evidence.label: A sports writer reconsiders the coverage · Comment · Dave Kidd
evidence.text: Kidd welcomed Sterling’s challenge and acknowledged unfair reporting. He defended the tattoo as a legitimate topic while saying he would not have made it the front-page lead. He called for greater diversity and dialogue in sports journalism. This is the named writer’s argument, not an unsigned leader or a statement by the owner. Its online date precedes the next day’s reported leader; disagreement is documented, but private editorial discussions are not reconstructed here.

evidence.label: Lineker challenges the coverage
evidence.text: Praises Sterling’s work ethic and condemns his treatment, linking Keyworth’s thread. Displayed timezone is not stated. Likes and reposts observed years later cannot establish the audience or pace of circulation during the 2018 window.

evidence.label: A headline-comparison thread
evidence.text: Collects examples of press treatment of Sterling in a critical headline-comparison thread. The preserved copy verifies this captured version, not a complete original archive of every image. Publication time has no established timezone. Capture time is not publication time. The live page’s unavailability does not establish why it disappeared.

evidence.label: The next day’s front page enters a social feed · original X post
evidence.text: Redistributes The Sun’s next-day Sterling front page under a newspaper-preview hashtag. The posting account is Henderson’s, not The Sun’s. Sharing the cover does not establish personal endorsement of its framing.

evidence.label: A radio guest’s target claim becomes a social clip · original X post
evidence.text: Promotes Dave Kitson’s comments that footballers should be careful with social media and can make themselves targets. The publisher’s caption is verified. Kitson’s claim is attributed opinion, not a justification for racist abuse. Upload time is not the original radio airtime; the full discussion was not transcribed.

evidence.label: Chelsea announces sanctions after the December match · 2019-07-30
evidence.text: Chelsea said it permanently excluded one spectator for racially abusive language and threatening or aggressive behaviour, and temporarily excluded five others for abusive behaviour. It described its evidence process and appeal rights. A club ticketing decision under a civil standard, not a criminal conviction or a finding about press coverage. The statement does not say all six used racist language. The CPS did not bring criminal prosecutions.

evidence.label: Leveson: later ethical comparison
evidence.text: This selected campaign postdates Leveson’s 2012 report. The report made no findings about it; its discussion can inform a comparison of evidence, dignity, privacy and editorial judgment.

evidence.label: Settlement statement filed as Document 78-1
evidence.text: The 15 February 2022 civil settlement did not adjudicate the allegations and contained no admission of liability. Andrew denied the allegations. This case must not be described as a conviction.

evidence.label: The Lord Archer of Weston-Super-Mare, House of Lords Hansard
evidence.text: Archer was convicted on 19 July 2001 and sentenced to four years. The House of Lords recorded the court clerk’s notice on 23 July. An obituary is a different editorial event from sentencing.

evidence.label: Gemma White KC's Report into the BBC's response to claims over Tim Westwood's Conduct
evidence.text: The 2025 review records informal handling of workplace concerns, weak records and missed opportunities. It also found very little evidence that public sexual-misconduct concerns had been reported to the BBC. This supports a specific institutional-response comparison, not a claim that all allegations were known or that no journalism occurred.

evidence.label: BBC publishes Board-commissioned review into Tim Westwood's conduct
evidence.text: The Board accepted the review and apologised. Its qualification about no widespread or significant knowledge concerns predatory sexual behaviour; internal workplace concerns are a distinct record.

evidence.label: Metropolitan Police Service charges Tim Westwood with further offences
evidence.text: On 22 September 2026 the Met announced two further charges, taking the total to 17. Charges are allegations, not convictions; the original trial was scheduled for January 2027. No plea on the two new charges is established by this record.

evidence.label: IICSA: the 1979 Rochdale Alternative Paper articles
evidence.text: IICSA recorded local articles in May and June 1979, followed by no major-national-newspaper pickup of those allegations. Private Eye and the New Statesman were exceptions. It contacted national papers’ archives without resolving why the story was not taken up. This is documented non-pickup, not an inference from empty searches.

evidence.label: IICSA report publication record
evidence.text: The official report was published 12 April 2018. Its findings about 1979 are retrospective.

evidence.label: Exclusive: Nigel Farage filmed undercover celebrating secret new foreign donations
evidence.text: Channel 4 News original page (opened in Chrome, displayed 3 Sep 2026) says it independently verified footage produced by Verbatim. It reports that a US company paid £32,500 for three Reform-commissioned polls, and that a future £500,000 donation was proposed via a UK-based son using funds from his US-based father. The larger transfer was never made. At a late-July meeting, Farage praised the polls and thanked the undercover team. Channel 4 says Reform did not comment before broadcast and later states the subjects deny the allegations. Original Channel 4 News page opened in Chrome; displayed date and full article read. Official associated YouTube video separately verified: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aXut3s90rUI

evidence.text: Current official list says Nigel Farage MP, opened 13 May 2026, Rule 5: failure to register an interest. This listed inquiry concerns the gift/register question; do not conflate it with the later party-funding police investigation. evidence.label: Register of Interests for Nigel Farage MP
evidence.text: Current register lists disclosed benefits including a £25,000 flight seat from Harborne for a February 2026 visit; the page's current categories and content are not a formal finding about the separate £5m 2024 gift. evidence.label: Metropolitan Police statement on Reform UK donations/polling reports
evidence.text: ITV original page opened in Chrome, dated 9 September 2026, reproduces the Met statement: after the 3 September Channel 4 broadcast, police assessed reports and identified potential offences requiring investigation, to be added to the existing Special Enquiry Team investigation into donations to the same party. Met says allegations concern potential offences under PPERA 2000 and detectives are seeking broadcast footage. Reform says it denies wrongdoing and will cooperate. ITV page opened in Chrome; title/date and Met spokesperson statement verified in page body

evidence.label: Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000, Part IV
evidence.text: Section 54 defines permissible donors (including an individual registered on an electoral register); sections 50 and 55 address what counts as a party donation, including indirect benefits and third-party spending to meet party expenses; section 61 addresses knowing arrangements facilitating donations from impermissible donors. An overseas residence alone does not establish that a donor is impermissible. Whether the reported facts meet these rules is for investigators/courts, not this evidence summary. Sections 50, 54, 55 and 61; legislation page says updated through 3 October 2026

evidence.label: Electoral Commission donations search: Christopher Harborne
evidence.text: Official Commission search export contained 47 records associated with Harborne's registered party donations on the 23 September 2026 export. evidence.label: Former UKIP MEP jailed for taking bribes
evidence.text: CPS records that former Reform Wales leader Nathan Gill pleaded guilty to eight bribery counts and was sentenced to 10.5 years in November 2025 for payments tied to conduct in the European Parliament in 2018–19. This conviction is a separate case and is not proof about Farage, the Harborne gift, or the September 2026 allegations. CPS press release

evidence.label: William O’Reilly: an education-panel comparison with missing public reasons
evidence.text: The current comparison bundle has an O’Reilly sample of one Varsity news report, one Per Capita report and one separately classified Varsity opinion in 29 September–5 October 2023, plus a separate June 2023 FT initial report whose original article metadata/body was not independently recovered. The bundle marks coverage unmeasured and notes no named official panel decision/full reasons. This is not a coverage census. Cross-check against local comparison-bundles.json, comparison-oreilly; Varsity story is linked as public anchor

evidence.label: Nigel Farage and Reform UK: political-finance scrutiny · source audit
evidence.text: Political finance has a strong public-interest claim: these reports concern a political leader’s large donor relationship, election funding and alleged concealment. The April personal-gift disclosure and September undercover investigation are separate episodes. Parliamentary and police inquiries are not findings of guilt. The recovered sample is not a measure of total attention or proof that the university case received disproportionate coverage. The verified seven-day September sample contains five news reports, one institutional editorial and one official Channel 4 video, with search-only candidates excluded. O’Reilly’s seven-day sample contains two news reports and one opinion. These are different selected outlet samples, not complete or matched censuses. They show that political-finance scrutiny occurred, but cannot establish relative attention. Power over public decisions, electoral integrity, sums involved and credible new evidence support sustained scrutiny; a criminal conviction is not a prerequisite for public-interest reporting. Fair reporting must also preserve denials, distinguish suspicion from proof, and update outcomes.

evidence.label: Cardiff REACH media monitoring report (2011)
evidence.text: Cardiff REACH report (2011): 66.9% of 499 sampled items featuring Black males aged11–24 were crime-related, compared with41.9% for all young men/boys, not white-only. Eight two-week monitoring windows,2008–09; news in print, TV and radio. Victims were included. This is historical content analysis, not a measure of the present cases or evidence of each editor’s intent.

evidence.label: Black British Voices Project (2023)
evidence.text: Cambridge/Voice/I-Cubed Black British Voices (2023), over10,000 respondents: three in four believed Black businesses were treated unfairly by investors and financial institutions. The report describes perceived media stereotyping and football double standards. Survey/interviews are evidence of respondents’ experiences and perceptions, not a content audit or a causal finding for these cases.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: In this fictional exercise, our desk accounts for 9 of the 15 retained records in a four-outlet sample spanning 28 May to 16 December. The May tattoo coverage and December debate about racialised portrayals concern different moments; each item needs its own public-interest justification.

We would also say context matters: Sterling connected the tattoo to his father’s killing and said it was unfinished. In December, he alleged that media framing could fuel racism after an alleged incident; we would label that as his claim, not a proven causal finding. We would link his post and the publisher’s response.

Across our sample, the story moved from an image and explanation to a wider question about representation. We would argue that scrutiny can be valuable when it examines institutions and language rather than turning a person into a symbol. We would not claim these headlines prove racist intent or explain the alleged abuse.

The retained sample is selected and incomplete. We would distinguish direct publisher pages from the Sun print headline reproduced by the Guardian, identify the format and dates, and state that the comparator stories concern other Manchester City players. These records do not prove racist intent or that headlines caused abuse.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: In this fictional exercise, our desk accounts for 3 of the 15 retained records in a four-outlet sample spanning 28 May to 16 December. The May tattoo coverage and December debate about racialised portrayals concern different moments; each item needs its own public-interest justification.

The tattoo image could prompt criticism, but Sterling’s explanation—that it commemorated his father, who was killed by gun violence—was essential context. In December he alleged that media portrayals of Black players can feed racist behaviour. We would keep that allegation distinct from proof of a causal link or a finding about any reporter’s intent.

Our responsibility is to report a public figure’s stated explanation and the debate without flattening two different episodes into one accusation. We would correct any implication that the tattoo endorses violence and avoid implying that headlines caused the alleged abuse.

The retained sample is selected and incomplete. We would distinguish direct publisher pages from the Sun print headline reproduced by the Guardian, identify the format and dates, and state that the comparator stories concern other Manchester City players. These records do not prove racist intent or that headlines caused abuse.

One is a web report published on 28 May; the other is a 29 May print headline reproduced in a contemporaneous report. A responsible account should place his explanation near the top: he connected the image to his father’s killing and said he would never touch a gun. Our defence is that the image and public criticism were already a live World Cup story, and the web report included campaigners’ objections and Sterling’s response. We should still examine whether the headline gave too much weight to outrage and whether the opening gave enough weight to his explanation. That is the strongest question these records raise about our choices.

The limit is clear: two items cannot show all our coverage, readers’ reactions, or whether a headline influenced the later alleged abuse. The print wording is a contemporaneous reproduction, not an original page. The comparison involving other players cannot establish our motive or prove a causal link. briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: In this fictional exercise, our one retained report was published on 29 May, as the tattoo story drew criticism. Its headline foregrounds the Football Association’s support after the row, while the article reports Sterling’s explanation and the FA response. We would defend covering a public controversy when an England player and the governing body had addressed it.

The strongest challenge is whether the headline gave readers enough context. A reference to a ‘gun tattoo row’ can leave the image and conflict in the foreground, even when the article explains Sterling’s personal reason. We should ask whether the headline and opening made that explanation visible, rather than assuming that context later in the article corrects the first impression.

Our answer is that reporting the FA’s support added a distinct, attributable development. We should include Sterling’s account that the tattoo connected to his father’s killing, and avoid presenting the image as evidence that he supported gun use. Readers can understand both the criticism and his explanation without being asked to hold one view of the tattoo.

The specific limit is that one dated page is one record in an incomplete sample. It cannot establish how this desk covered the story on other days, how its audience reacted, or whether its wording was fair across all formats. The later allegation about abuse and debate about newspaper framing are separate developments; this report cannot establish motive or causation. We would make those boundaries clear whenever we cite the sample.

publicContext.intro: Raheem Sterling was an England and Manchester City footballer whose tattoo, spending and experiences of racism drew coverage in 2018. An alleged racist-abuse incident on 8 December was followed by his public criticism of newspaper framing on 9 December. Examine whether coverage investigated racism, repeated personal judgment or helped readers understand the wider issue.
publicContext.allegationResponse: The recovered sample includes criticism of newspaper coverage as well as reports about Sterling. It does not measure every article about him.

representationResearch.title: When an individual story becomes a racial pattern
representationResearch.interpretation: A defensible initial story does not settle whether selection, repeated framing, prominence and persistence produce unequal treatment. Structural bias can be examined without an editor admitting intent. A deliberate strategy to conceal bias is a separate claim requiring evidence.

studies.label: Cardiff REACH media monitoring report (2011)
studies.text: Cardiff REACH report (2011): 66.9% of 499 sampled items featuring Black males aged11–24 were crime-related, compared with41.9% for all young men/boys, not white-only. Eight two-week monitoring windows,2008–09; news in print, TV and radio. Victims were included. This is historical content analysis, not a measure of the present cases or evidence of each editor’s intent.
studies.finding: Crime accounted for 66.9% of sampled items featuring Black young men and boys, against 41.9% for all young men and boys.
studies.limit: The comparator includes Black youth; the sample is from 2008–09 and includes victims. It does not mean 67% portrayed Black people as criminals.

studies.label: Black British Voices Project (2023)
studies.text: Cambridge/Voice/I-Cubed Black British Voices (2023), over10,000 respondents: three in four believed Black businesses were treated unfairly by investors and financial institutions. The report describes perceived media stereotyping and football double standards. Survey/interviews are evidence of respondents’ experiences and perceptions, not a content audit or a causal finding for these cases.
studies.finding: Three in four respondents believed Black businesses were treated unfairly by investors and financial institutions. Media stereotyping and football double standards were also concerns in the report.
studies.limit: A survey and interviews document reported experience and perceptions. Business-investment findings cannot be relabelled as a measured media-coverage disparity.
studies.locator: Business/enterprise and media chapters; University of Cambridge summary.

industrySource.label: NCTJ Diversity in Journalism (2023)
industrySource.finding: Its 2022 data estimated that 88% of UK journalists were White. Workforce representation is relevant context; this statistic alone does not demonstrate a newsroom’s bias.

attributionCorrections: The crime statistic is from Cardiff’s REACH report, not a verified Reuters study.
The Lammy Review concerns criminal-justice disparities. The cited wealth-and-driving claim is not established by that review; separate Liberty/StopWatch work addresses traffic stops.
questions: Did criticism of a specific act become a fixed judgment about the whole person?
Did money, dress, cars or ambition become a reason to portray someone as undeserving?
Was an allegation repeatedly recalled after its status changed, without new information?
Were replies, achievements and ordinary context given similar prominence?
Would the same conduct, evidence and public role have attracted similar persistence and framing for someone else?
representationResearch.claimBoundary: Neither serious allegations nor proven wrongdoing gives an outlet unlimited permission for humiliation. Fair scrutiny of alleged abuse also protects complainants; the question is how the coverage treats evidence, power and people.
